paragraphs: Reconstructing how cells change over time is difficult when measurements destroy the cells being observed. Researchers must connect separate snapshots while accounting for random changes, cell division, and cell death. Existing unbalanced optimal transport methods represent changing cell populations as continuous mass, which can obscure the individual birth and death events that produce branching lineages.

Unbalanced Schrödinger Bridge, or USB, instead gives the dynamics an individual-cell interpretation. Cells undergo both Brownian motion and discrete birth–death jumps. The framework provides a tractable solution to the Branching Schrödinger Bridge problem, connecting population-level observations with a microscopic account of how cells move, multiply, and disappear. Its training objective avoids simulation and is designed to scale to high-dimensional omics measurements.

On simulated and real datasets, USB reconstructs trajectories better than or comparably to deterministic baselines. The additional contribution is its ability to simulate discrete birth–death events at single-cell resolution. Simulation-free training therefore supports a model that can subsequently generate branching cellular dynamics, rather than only describe population movement.
icml-2026-beyond-continuity-simulation-f.tldr: USB learns cellular trajectories from snapshots while explicitly modeling random movement and discrete cell birth and death.

paragraphs: Personalized federated learning lets clients share information while retaining models suited to their own data. A collaboration graph determines how their models are combined. This paper analyzes why that process can lose its personalized structure: excessive collaboration pushes everyone toward one model, while repeatedly strengthening connections between similar clients can split the network into isolated groups.

The theoretical analysis shows that, with the same budget of representative models, collaborative personalization is more expressive and offers higher-order approximation accuracy than clustered personalization. A bound on model disagreement explains how this advantage can disappear through consensus or self-clustering. The proposed pFedCCG method controls the collaboration structure to preserve that advantage.

pFedCCG starts with a similarity template fixed independently of training. It optimizes a Markovian collaboration matrix with a prescribed stationary distribution, using reversible parameterization and projection, and schedules collaboration strength. Experiments across different forms of client heterogeneity report consistent personalization improvements and substantially less collapse and self-clustering. The findings support controlling how collaboration evolves as part of personalization.
icml-2026-controlled-collaboration-geome.tldr: pFedCCG controls client collaboration to improve personalized federated learning while reducing consensus collapse and self-clustering.

paragraphs: A classifier can express uncertainty by predicting a distribution over possible class-probability vectors. However, making that distribution more flexible does not necessarily clarify where uncertainty comes from or how different sources are combined. This paper introduces a courtroom analogy to make the internal structure of an uncertainty estimate easier to interpret.

Each class has an advocate that supplies a probabilistic opinion. The final prediction combines those opinions using plausibility weights that depend on the input. Each opinion is a Dirichlet distribution, with its concentration parameters divided into shared evidence and class-specific advocacy. Together, these components form a structured mixture whose parameters have explicit roles in representing and aggregating uncertainty.

The authors implement this formulation as Mixture of Dirichlet EXperts, or MoDEX. A single neural-network pass predicts the courtroom parameters, combining efficient inference with a flexible uncertainty representation. The paper reports strong theoretical properties and state-of-the-art uncertainty quantification across diverse benchmarks. Its central contribution is to make the combination of competing class opinions part of the model's interpretable structure.
icml-2026-courtroom-analogy-new-perspect.tldr: MoDEX produces interpretable uncertainty estimates by combining class-specific probabilistic opinions in a single neural-network pass.

paragraphs: Robotic planning benefits from world models that predict how a scene will change, but dense Transformer models can be expensive to run. DDP-WM starts from the hypothesis that different parts of a scene need different kinds of prediction. Physical interactions drive sparse primary changes, while surrounding context requires secondary background updates.

The architecture separates these two kinds of dynamics. It processes historical information efficiently and localizes the primary changes, then uses cross-attention to update the background. This division allocates computation according to the proposed structure of scene evolution. The framework also provides a smooth optimization landscape for planners, connecting prediction efficiency with the process of choosing actions.

Experiments cover navigation, precise tabletop manipulation, and deformable or multi-body interactions, with reported improvements in both efficiency and performance. On Push-T, DDP-WM runs inference approximately nine times faster than the compared state-of-the-art dense models and increases model predictive control success from 90% to 98%. These results support the proposed decomposition across the evaluated tasks without establishing that every scene follows it.
icml-2026-ddp-wm-disentangled-dynamics-p.tldr: DDP-WM separates primary physical dynamics from background updates to make robotic world models faster and more effective.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning depends on how an agent receives observations and expresses actions, as well as on the rewards it receives. Those observation and action spaces are often designed through human intuition. LOAM explores using language models to refine these interfaces, extending automated environment design beyond the reward functions that have received most prior attention.

The framework asks language models to construct observation and action models from raw environments. Because language-model generation is stochastic, it can produce multiple candidate configurations, making selection computationally demanding. LOAM addresses this with continuous racing: it dynamically directs resources toward the configurations that look most promising, with the stated aim of selecting candidates without additional training overhead.

Evaluations on HumanoidBench and Isaac Lab show consistent improvements over handcrafted baselines in both learning speed and eventual performance. The findings suggest that language models can contribute useful design choices about the information and controls exposed to an agent. The racing mechanism matters because it makes searching among these generated designs part of an efficient learning workflow.
icml-2026-designing-observation-and-acti.tldr: LOAM uses language models and adaptive candidate selection to design observation and action spaces that improve reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: Some multimodal models reason through intermediate images as well as text, using crops, annotations, spatial localization, or sketches. Evaluating only their written reasoning leaves a gap: a textual explanation can depend on an incorrect visual operation. This paper develops a process reward model that can assess both kinds of intermediate steps.

DiscPRM evaluates visual reasoning trajectories, the image operations within them, and consistency between text and images. To train this capability, the authors construct VTReward-100K, a dataset containing supervised sequences of visual reasoning steps. The focus is on judging the process as it unfolds, including whether the visual evidence and accompanying explanation fit together.

When used to supervise Best-of-N selection among candidate reasoning processes, DiscPRM produces reported gains of over 5% across benchmarks requiring visual intermediate steps. The paper also introduces VABench to evaluate process reward models on detecting visual reasoning errors. Together, the model, training data, and benchmark extend process supervision to reasoning whose correctness depends on what happens inside intermediate images.
icml-2026-discriminative-visual-process-.tldr: DiscPRM evaluates intermediate visual and textual reasoning steps, improving candidate selection on tasks that require thinking with images.

paragraphs: Models that update as data arrive must distinguish unusual observations from genuine changes in the underlying regime. This paper develops a robust update rule for an online infinite hidden Markov model when the stream contains outliers and the assumed model does not perfectly match the data. Both problems can affect forecasting and interpretation.

The method uses generalized Bayesian inference and defines robustness through the posterior influence function, which describes how observations affect the posterior. The authors give conditions under which this influence remains bounded. They also identify a cost of robustness: resisting unusual observations inevitably delays adaptation when the underlying regime actually changes.

Batched Robust iHMM, or BR-iHMM, balances that trade-off with two additional tunable parameters. Experiments use limit order book data, hourly electricity demand, and a synthetic high-dimensional linear system. The method reduces one-step-ahead forecasting error by up to 67% compared with competing online Bayesian approaches. That reported maximum, together with the conditional robustness guarantees, supports its practical use where resistance to outliers must coexist with adaptation.
icml-2026-doubly-outlier-robust-online-i.tldr: BR-iHMM balances resistance to outliers and model mismatch against the delay this robustness introduces when regimes change.

paragraphs: Having several language models debate an answer can improve reasoning, but interaction is not equally useful in every setting. The paper draws on a distinction between corrective dynamics, where interaction amplifies useful information, and symmetric dynamics, which are neutral in expectation. In the latter case, majority voting may be preferable to spending tokens on discussion.

LASE, short for Leader-Adaptive Structured Engagement, makes the decision to debate part of the framework. It uses a leader–supporter structure to direct information flow and selectively amplify useful signals. Interaction is engaged only in regimes identified as non-neutral; otherwise, the system falls back to simple aggregation. This combines selective participation with an intentionally asymmetric discussion structure.

Across diverse reasoning benchmarks, LASE achieves performance associated with multi-agent systems while using close to a single agent's token budget. It also improves efficiency over static debate and voting baselines. The findings support the paper's central argument that the value of debate depends on when it is invoked and how information moves between participants.
icml-2026-efficient-multi-agent-reasonin.tldr: LASE selectively organizes leader–supporter debate to achieve multi-agent reasoning performance at near single-agent token cost.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards trains language models using feedback that can be checked, making it useful for mathematical reasoning. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning reduces how much of a model must be updated, but the paper asks whether the commonly chosen LoRA architecture is the best fit for this training setting.

The authors evaluate more than twelve parameter-efficient methods across DeepSeek-R1-Distill model families on mathematical reasoning benchmarks. Structural alternatives including DoRA, AdaLoRA, and MiSS consistently outperform standard LoRA in these experiments. This makes the structure of the trainable update an important empirical choice, rather than treating all small updates as interchangeable.

The study also finds spectral collapse in SVD-informed initialization methods such as PiSSA and MiLoRA, attributing their failures to a mismatch between principal-component updates and reinforcement-learning optimization. Ablations show that extreme parameter reductions, including VeRA and Rank-1, severely constrain reasoning capacity. Further ablation and scaling experiments support these findings. The practical implication is to assess parameter efficiency alongside optimization compatibility and retained reasoning capacity.
icml-2026-evaluating-parameter-efficient.tldr: An evaluation of parameter-efficient RLVR methods finds stronger alternatives to LoRA and identifies failures from unsuitable initialization and extreme parameter reduction.

paragraphs: Reconstructing a 3D scene from only a few images leaves regions insufficiently constrained, often producing artifacts in Gaussian Splatting representations. Generative models can help complete those regions, but their additions may disagree with the original observations. GSFixer addresses this by using the sparse input views as explicit references during restoration.

Its core is a video restoration model built on a diffusion Transformer and trained with paired artifact-containing renders and clean frames. Reference conditions combine 2D semantic features with 3D geometric features extracted by a visual geometry foundation model. These signals guide repairs toward content that is coherent in meaning and consistent with the scene's geometry.

GSFixer also samples viewing trajectories with reference guidance to provide angular coverage while maintaining view quality. The authors introduce DL3DV-Res, a benchmark containing artifact frames rendered from low-quality Gaussian Splatting reconstructions. Experiments report improvements over current state-of-the-art methods in both artifact restoration and sparse-view reconstruction. The contribution links generative repair to observed evidence at both the feature and viewpoint-selection levels.
icml-2026-gsfixer-improving-3d-gaussian-.tldr: GSFixer uses reference-guided video diffusion to repair sparse-view Gaussian Splatting reconstructions while improving consistency with observed images.

paragraphs: Masked diffusion language models generate text through repeated updates to masked tokens, allowing parallel decoding and access to context in both directions. However, updating several tokens simultaneously introduces factorization errors. These errors make it difficult to produce good outputs in very few sampling steps, even though parallel generation is a central attraction of the approach.

The paper identifies a theoretical lower bound on this error that standard masked diffusion models cannot reduce because they use one deterministic mask state. Infinite Mask Diffusion replaces that state with a stochastic mask having infinitely many possible states. The proposed model retains the advantages of distinguishing masked positions from data and remains compatible with pretrained weights.

On a simple synthetic task, standard masked diffusion fails at few-step generation because of the identified error bound, while the new model finds an efficient solution. With appropriate distillation methods, it also outperforms existing few-step distillation approaches at small step counts on LM1B and OpenWebText. The result ties faster generation to changing the mask representation itself.
icml-2026-infinite-mask-diffusion-for-fe.tldr: Infinite Mask Diffusion replaces a single deterministic mask state with stochastic mask states to improve few-step text generation.

paragraphs: Reasoning in an unfamiliar environment requires choosing what to investigate, interpreting the results, and revising explanations. The Oracle benchmark evaluates this integrated process through black-box interaction. Each black box hides a function mapping inputs to outputs, and the model must discover that function through a limited number of exploration turns.

The benchmark contains 96 black boxes across six task types and evaluates nineteen language models. Because models decide how to interact with the hidden function, the tasks bring together deduction, induction, and abduction. Success depends on both reasoning about observed input–output pairs and gathering observations that help distinguish competing hypotheses.

Among the evaluated models, o3 ranks first on five of the six tasks and exceeds 70% accuracy on most easy black boxes. Its average performance nevertheless falls below 40% on some hard tasks. Further analysis identifies a shared difficulty among the tested models: planning efficient, adaptive exploration for hypothesis refinement. The benchmark therefore exposes weaknesses in directing an investigation, beyond interpreting evidence already provided.
icml-2026-investigating-advanced-reasoni.tldr: Oracle tests whether language models can discover hidden functions through interaction, revealing weaknesses in adaptive exploration and hypothesis refinement.

paragraphs: Neuro-fuzzy systems aim to combine learned prediction with rules whose meaning people can inspect. Conventional Adaptive Neuro-Fuzzy Inference Systems face a scaling problem: their product-based inference can cause the number of rules to grow exponentially as input dimensionality increases. KANFIS changes the architecture to keep this rule-based approach more compact.

The proposed Kolmogorov-Arnold Neuro-Fuzzy Inference System combines fuzzy reasoning with additive function decomposition. Under its additive aggregation mechanism, both parameter count and rule complexity grow linearly with input dimensionality. Sparse masks further produce compact, structured rule sets, supporting clear rule semantics and a transparent inference process within the model itself.

KANFIS supports both Type-1 and Interval Type-2 fuzzy logic, allowing uncertainty and ambiguity to be represented explicitly in its fuzzy components. Experiments find competitive performance against representative neural and neuro-fuzzy baselines. The stated result is a combination of manageable structural growth, interpretable reasoning, and competitive predictive performance, rather than a claim that interpretability requires sacrificing accuracy or that the model universally outperforms alternatives.
icml-2026-kanfis-a-neuro-symbolic-framew.tldr: KANFIS combines additive decomposition and fuzzy rules to provide interpretable, uncertainty-aware learning with linear structural growth.

paragraphs: Multi-objective reinforcement learning must account for several goals at once, while risk-sensitive learning also considers uncertainty in outcomes. This paper brings those requirements together through distributional reinforcement learning. Its framework uses vector-risk measures to represent risk across multiple objectives, with finance and robotics identified as potential application domains.

The method approximates these measures using Knothe-Rosenblatt quantile regression, extending the IQN framework to multiple objectives. The construction aligns with the axiomatic definition of vector-risk measures, and the paper establishes critic convergence under the distributional Bellman operator. This gives the proposed representation a theoretical connection to both risk measurement and the update rule used to learn outcome distributions.

The Knothe-Rosenblatt map imposes an artificial ordering, so the authors use a Transformer without positional encoding to mitigate that effect. They also introduce MO-TQC to improve training stability. Experiments report improved performance on MO-Gymnasium benchmarks and examine risk-sensitive policies in multi-objective tasks. The contribution provides a way to study preferences over uncertain outcomes when several objectives must be considered together.
icml-2026-knothe-rosenblatt-quantile-reg.tldr: The paper extends distributional reinforcement learning to multiple objectives using quantile regression and vector-valued risk measures.

paragraphs: Understanding a scene over time requires reasoning about how three-dimensional space changes from one moment to the next. MLLM-4D targets this capability in multimodal language models using visual inputs. It addresses both the supply of suitable instructional data and the post-training process used to teach spatial and temporal reasoning.

The data pipeline repurposes existing stereo video datasets into instructions about space and time. It produces MLLM4D-2M for supervised fine-tuning, MLLM4D-R1-30k for reinforcement fine-tuning, and MLLM4D-Bench for evaluation. Reusing stereo video provides a cost-efficient route to constructing training material for a capability that the paper identifies as a bottleneck.

Training first establishes foundational understanding through supervised fine-tuning. A second stage uses Group Relative Policy Optimization with specialized spatiotemporal chain-of-thought prompts and rewards to develop reasoning further. This process does not require architectural modifications. Experiments report state-of-the-art spatial-temporal understanding and reasoning from purely 2D RGB inputs, supporting the value of combining targeted data curation with specialized post-training for reasoning about 3D scenes over time.
icml-2026-mllm-4d-towards-visual-based-s.tldr: MLLM-4D combines curated video instruction data and specialized post-training to improve reasoning about 3D space over time from RGB inputs.

paragraphs: When humans work with increasingly accurate AI, paying for correct outputs can become a poor way to encourage costly human effort. This paper studies that problem in a budget-constrained principal–agent model where effort is hidden and influences output accuracy. It establishes that incentive collapse extends to any payment rule based only on observed task accuracy.

The proposed remedy is a sentinel-auditing payment mechanism. Within the studied framework, it sustains a strictly positive, controllable amount of human effort at finite cost, independently of AI accuracy. This addresses the incentive problem before optimizing which tasks to assign or how much information to collect from them.

The authors then develop an active statistical inference framework that jointly chooses the auditing rate, task sampling, and budget allocation across tasks of different difficulty. All these decisions share one budget and aim to minimize final statistical loss. Experiments show improved cost–error trade-offs over standard active learning and auditing-only baselines. The result connects reliable effort incentives with efficient information gathering under a common resource constraint.
icml-2026-overcoming-the-incentive-colla.tldr: Sentinel auditing sustains human effort at finite cost in the studied delegation model and improves budget allocation for statistical inference.

paragraphs: Text-to-music diffusion models can produce limited patterns even when prompts and initial noise vary. Increasing diversity during sampling can also disrupt prompt cues established early in denoising, weakening text alignment and fidelity. PADS-TAL addresses this trade-off by controlling both where sampling perturbations occur and how the latent space organizes musical variation.

Padding-Annealed Diffusion Sampling perturbs only a padding-indexed subspace while holding non-padding conditioning fixed. This enables exploration with less semantic drift. The authors then introduce a Text-Aware Latent space whose local neighborhoods reflect the genre structure implied by text, making exploration more likely to remain consistent with the requested genre.

Together, the techniques improve the alignment–diversity trade-off compared with methods that perturb the full conditioning. At comparable text alignment, the pipeline yields 15.4% higher diversity with a relatively small fidelity decrease, and it further improves within-genre diversity by 71.6%. The findings preserve an explicit trade-off: greater variety still carries some fidelity cost, while the proposed design better maintains the prompt's musical direction.
icml-2026-pads-tal-padding-annealed-diff.tldr: PADS-TAL increases text-to-music diversity through selective perturbations and genre-aware latent neighborhoods while better preserving text alignment.

paragraphs: Generative Flow Networks sample diverse candidates in proportion to a reward, making them useful when scientific discovery requires exploring several promising solutions. Multiple objectives complicate this process because their rewards may conflict. Existing approaches described in the paper require joint training for each objective combination, making changes to the objective set expensive.

The proposed framework composes pretrained GFlowNets during inference, allowing objective combinations to change without fine-tuning or retraining. It supports both linear weighted combinations and more complex nonlinear operators. This flexibility lets the same composition framework address reward combinations that earlier work often treated separately.

The theoretical results distinguish these cases carefully: the method exactly recovers the target distribution for linear scalarization, while a distortion factor quantifies approximation quality for nonlinear combinations. Experiments on a synthetic two-dimensional grid and molecule generation tasks achieve performance comparable to baselines. The practical contribution is therefore adaptable multi-objective generation with competitive results, alongside exactness for linear combinations and a quantified approximation for nonlinear ones.
icml-2026-routing-by-reaching-compositio.tldr: The framework combines pretrained GFlowNets at inference time to handle changing objectives without retraining, with exact recovery for linear reward combinations.

paragraphs: Speculative decoding speeds up language-model generation by having a draft model propose tokens for a larger target model to verify. Judge decoding relaxes this verification, allowing minor differences from the target's output. However, existing judge-training methods depend on human annotations or tasks with verifiable answers, restricting where they can be applied.

SelfJudge trains these verifiers through self-supervision from the target model. It evaluates whether responses with substituted tokens preserve the meaning of the original responses. This semantic-preservation signal supplies automatic training information for the judge, allowing verifier training across diverse natural-language tasks without relying on the same task-specific sources of supervision.

Experiments report better inference–accuracy trade-offs than judge-decoding baselines. The significance is that a judge can learn which token differences are acceptable from signals supplied by the target model itself. The resulting approach broadens the applicability of relaxed verification while retaining accuracy as part of the evaluation, rather than treating generation speed as the only objective.
icml-2026-selfjudge-faster-speculative-d.tldr: SelfJudge trains speculative-decoding verifiers from the target model's own semantic-preservation signals, improving inference–accuracy trade-offs.

paragraphs: Searching for wording variations in enormous text collections is harder than finding exact strings. SoftMatcha 2 permits substitutions, insertions, and deletions while using word vectors to support semantic flexibility. The paper reports searches over trillion-scale corpora in under 0.3 seconds, bringing flexible pattern matching to collections where search cost is a central concern.

The algorithm combines suffix-array string matching with two mechanisms for controlling the expanded search space. Dynamic corpus-aware pruning limits the possibilities considered, while a disk-aware design enables fast exact lookups. The theoretical analysis indicates that these mechanisms can mitigate the exponential search-space growth introduced by relaxing a query.

On the 1.4-trillion-token FineWeb-Edu corpus, SoftMatcha 2 achieves substantially lower latency than infini-gram, infini-gram mini, and the original SoftMatcha. It also identifies benchmark contamination missed by existing approaches and benefits retrieval and paraphrase detection. An online demonstration covers corpora in seven languages. These applications show why allowing textual variation matters: relevant matches can survive changes that prevent exact wording from being found.
icml-2026-softmatcha-2-a-fast-and-soft-p.tldr: SoftMatcha 2 enables fast semantic pattern matching over trillion-scale text collections through corpus-aware pruning and efficient indexed lookup.

paragraphs: A long movie summary and a short clip's object count demand different visual evidence. Task-Aware Mechanism, or TAM, adapts how many video frames are processed and at what resolution according to the question and video length. Its aim is to allocate visual processing to the temporal and spatial details that a task needs.

A compact 0.1-billion-parameter text-only Inductor, trained on TA-116K, infers the task type. That decision guides visual budgeting and routing through a hybrid mixture-of-experts vision tower. The encoder uses soft gating for stability, while resolution-specific projectors and pipelines use hard gating for efficient specialization. Separating task classification from subsequent visual-language reasoning also makes routing choices easier to inspect.

Built on Qwen2-7B, the resulting TallVA-8B-A7B model achieves state-of-the-art performance on most video benchmarks among models with comparable language-model backbones and remains competitive with stronger-backbone baselines. The explicit budget helps diagnose when a fixed pipeline misses temporal or spatial evidence. The results support matching visual processing to the question as a way to broaden video understanding.
icml-2026-task-aware-mechanism-hybrid-mo.tldr: TAM adapts video frame counts, resolution, and expert routing to the task, improving video understanding with inspectable visual budgets.

paragraphs: Diffusion models usually learn denoising targets at individual time steps or adjacent pairs of steps. These local objectives do not enforce agreement between predictions farther along the same denoising path. The paper argues that this inconsistency can harm generation, particularly when a sampler must reach its output in only a few steps.

The authors reformulate diffusion as a Markov reward process and treat denoising as a policy-evaluation problem from reinforcement learning. This leads to a temporal-difference objective that penalizes inconsistent multi-step progress. The formulation applies to both discrete-time and continuous-time diffusion, and a sample-based reweighting method is introduced to stabilize training.

Experiments show significant improvements in sample quality measured by FID, with larger advantages when sampling uses fewer steps. Ablations examine pairwise loss reweighting, regularization strength, and one-step stride. These findings support cross-time consistency as a useful training signal under limited inference computation. The proposed objective is presented as a potentially general addition to diffusion training across different generative models.
icml-2026-temporal-difference-learning-f.tldr: A temporal-difference training objective improves diffusion models by encouraging consistent multi-step denoising, with stronger gains for few-step sampling.

paragraphs: Multimodal representation learning places different kinds of data in a shared space so that related content aligns. This paper identifies two conflicts in InfoNCE-based training that can leave the modalities separated. Both become more pronounced as additional modalities are included, making the problem especially relevant beyond a simple pair of input types.

The first conflict is between alignment and uniformity: spreading representations apart can work against bringing matching examples together. The second occurs within alignment itself, as matching several modalities introduces competing directions. The authors propose separating alignment and uniformity to remove these identified conflicts while supporting both discriminative and generative uses without task-specific modules.

The theoretical analysis establishes that the method is an efficient proxy for a global Hölder divergence across modality distributions, providing a connection to reducing their distribution gap. Experiments on retrieval and UnCLIP-style generation report consistent gains. Together, the analysis and results suggest that coordinating the training objectives can improve a shared representation's usefulness for both finding related content and generating content.
icml-2026-towards-uniformity-and-alignme.tldr: Decoupling alignment and uniformity addresses competing multimodal training signals and improves retrieval and generation.

paragraphs: Infrared object detectors rely on thermal information, so physical adversarial patterns must affect heat signatures rather than ordinary color textures. This paper studies the shape of heat-blocking materials as the carrier of adversarial information. It identifies a trade-off in earlier shape-based approaches between representing expressive boundaries and optimizing those boundaries effectively.

The proposed method represents boundaries with a compact set of learnable Fourier coefficients. An analytic mapping based on the winding number theorem connects that representation to a pixel-space mask within a differentiable framework. This connection lets optimization adjust expressive shapes directly, addressing the representational and optimization constraints together.

Digital and physical experiments report stronger attack performance and robustness across changes in distance, viewing angle, pose, and individual. The physical patch exceeds an 88% attack success rate beyond 25 meters at a detector confidence threshold of 0.5. Those conditions are part of the reported result. The study demonstrates a physical vulnerability in the evaluated infrared detection settings and shows why geometric representation matters when adversarial information is carried by thermal obstruction.
icml-2026-unleashing-the-representationa.tldr: Learnable Fourier boundaries produce effective physical adversarial shapes for infrared detection, with robustness demonstrated across varied viewing conditions.

paragraphs: Detecting changes between visits to an indoor space is difficult when the camera follows different paths and many objects appear or disappear. VSCD defines this problem using reference and query RGB videos recorded at different times. The videos need not be synchronized, and the system predicts a pixel-level change mask for each query frame.

The authors build a benchmark with more than 1.1 million frames carrying pixel-accurate change annotations, plus a real-world test set for evaluating transfer beyond simulation. Their model uses multiple reference candidates for each query. It learns temporal matching implicitly from change-mask supervision and aligns reference features through local patch correspondence.

Frame-level and patch-level confidence guide the combination of candidate change features before one high-resolution mask is decoded per query frame. The approach achieves state-of-the-art performance against strong image-based and video-based baselines. Deployment on a mobile robot demonstrates use in visual surveillance and incremental object learning. The contribution brings change detection into a setting with unconstrained camera motion and substantial object changes.
icml-2026-vscd-video-based-scene-change-.tldr: VSCD detects pixel-level scene changes between unsynchronized indoor videos using multiple reference views and confidence-guided feature fusion.
